summary:
Casanare department stands under the national framework of Colombia, where the legal position a trans visitor meets is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015 the sex marker on government-issued identification has been changed by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments, and Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Further national provisions define the formal legal exposure of a visitor to the department. Homosexuality was decriminalised in 1981, and Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011. The Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in a 6-3 ruling of 28 April 2016, with the first wedding in Cali on 24 May 2016; three rulings between February 2007 and April 2008 had already granted same-sex couples property, social-security and pension rights, and a November 2015 ruling granted full adoption rights with dual-parent birth registration. Since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options: male, female and X. Adults can change legal gender before a notary without surgery, with a free simultaneous name change on first request. Gays, lesbians and bisexuals have served openly in the armed forces since a 1999 court ruling. Casanare adds no separate legal regime of its own.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence that a visitor should expect to encounter. CNN's 'As Equals' feature of 6 August 2025 documents continuing killings of LGBTQ+ people in Colombia after the Millerey case, with gangs linked to queer and transgender deaths. On 5 April 2025 a video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, drowning in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, after being thrown in unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands; her mother Sandra Borja said "They killed her for being who she was," President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed groups. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate there was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night, and a second trans woman said a friend was killed. Reporting gives eight trans women killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and states that discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. Casanare falls under these national kill figures and this armed-group pattern, with no Casanare-specific finding of its own.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

The armed-group 'social cleansing' campaigns documented in Caquetá and Guajira are the closest analogue to what a visitor to Casanare may face, since Casanare sits within the same pattern of conflict-era armed groups issuing public kill lists without a Casanare-specific finding. The national kill figures for trans women (41 in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, thirteen in the first quarter of 2025) are distributed across departments and do not isolate Casanare.

Colombia's legal reforms are frequently cited as a regional leader, a contrast drawn by the UN Independent Expert in May 2025 between institutional progress and lived experience. The gap between formal protection and daily safety is the central turbulence in the country's profile.
localsOnly:
Residents of Casanare use the same national routes as the rest of Colombia: sex marker changes before a notary since June 2015, free simultaneous name change on first request, and passports with male, female and X options since August 2023. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree and the May 2018 executive decree impose procedural obligations on government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons, housing, work, recreation, sports and culture, obligations that bind departments including Casanare.

Discrimination limits trans women in Colombia mainly to hairdressing or sex work, a labour-market pattern that would apply to Casanare residents as to those elsewhere.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Casanare-specific source finding exists in the inventory; the departmental entry yielded no usable content, and every claim above is drawn from national or other-department sources. Whether armed-group kill-list or 'social cleansing' flyer campaigns have appeared in Casanare itself is unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory does not resolve how many trans people were killed in Casanare specifically, or whether the department records any enforcement of the national anti-discrimination law of 2011.
